An ideal gas is defined by the assumption that its molecules exert no force on one another except during collisions, so there is no intermolecular potential-energy term. The whole of the internal energy is therefore the kinetic energy of the random molecular motion.

The chapter states this directly in \( \S \)3.7: "In an ideal gas, the molecules are noninteracting, and hence there is no potential energy term. Thus, the internal energy of an ideal gas is purely kinetic." Consistently, Eq. (3.17) gives the total energy of \( N \) molecules as \( E = \dfrac{3}{2} N k_{B} T \), a purely kinetic expression.

Options (B) and (C) both require a potential-energy term that the ideal-gas model excludes; option (D) would leave the molecules with no energy at all, contradicting the fact that they are in continuous random motion at any \( T > 0 \).

Hence the molecules possess only kinetic energy — option (A).

A molecule of diameter \( d \) collides with any molecule whose centre lies within a cylinder of cross-section \( \pi d^{2} \) swept along its path. Correcting for the fact that the other molecules are moving too introduces a factor \( \sqrt{2} \) in the relative speed, giving the chapter's Eq. (3.6):

\( \lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\, \pi d^{2} \left( \dfrac{N}{V} \right)} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\, \pi n d^{2}} \), with \( n = \dfrac{N}{V} \).

Discrimination. A mean free path must have the dimension of length. With \( [n] = L^{-3} \) and \( [d] = L \), option (A) has dimension \( L^{1/2} \) and is eliminated outright. Options (B), (C) and (D) are each a length, so dimension alone does not decide between them: (B) omits the \( \sqrt{2} \) relative-speed correction, and (D) has \( d \) to the first power inside a square root rather than \( d^{2} \), so it does not reproduce the collision cross-section \( \pi d^{2} \) at all.

Hence \( \lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\, \pi n d^{2}} \) — option (C).

The change is isothermal, so Boyle's law applies: \( P_{1} V_{1} = P_{2} V_{2} \).

The pressure falls by 10%, so \( P_{2} = 0.90\, P_{1} \).

\( V_{2} = \dfrac{P_{1} V_{1}}{P_{2}} = \dfrac{V_{1}}{0.90} = 1.1111\, V_{1} \)

The volume therefore INCREASES by \( 11.11\% \).

Discrimination — each option's claimed volume change implies a pressure ratio \( P_{2}/P_{1} = V_{1}/V_{2} \), and only one of them is \( 0.90 \): (A) a 9% decrease gives \( 1.0989 \) (a pressure rise, wrong sign); (B) a 9% increase gives \( 0.9174 \), a fall of only 8.26%; (C) a 10% decrease gives \( 1.1111 \), again a rise; (D) an 11.11% increase gives \( 0.9000 \) exactly.

Note that a 10% fall in pressure does not produce a 10% rise in volume — the relation is reciprocal, not linear, which is the trap options (B) and (C) are set for.

Hence the volume increases by 11.11% — option (D).

Of the total heat radiation incident on a body, one part is absorbed, one reflected and one transmitted. Dividing the energy-conservation statement \( Q_{a} + Q_{r} + Q_{t} = Q \) by \( Q \) gives the chapter's relation between the coefficient of absorption, of reflection and of transmission:

\( a + r + t_{\mathrm{r}} = 1 \)

Given \( a = 0.72 \) and \( r = 0.24 \),

\( t_{\mathrm{r}} = 1 - 0.72 - 0.24 = 0.04 \)

Discrimination — substituting each option back into \( a + r + t_{\mathrm{r}} \) gives 0.98 for (A), 1.00 for (B), 1.36 for (C) and 1.16 for (D). Only (B) satisfies the identity; the other three would require the body to absorb, reflect and transmit a total that is not the whole of the incident radiation.

Hence \( t_{\mathrm{r}} = 0.04 \) — option (B).

Stefan-Boltzmann law: the emissive power of a perfect blackbody is \( R = \sigma T^{4} \), with \( T \) the ABSOLUTE temperature. Convert both temperatures to kelvin first — this is the whole of the question.

\( T_{1} = 1327\ ^\circ \text{C} = 1327 + 273 = 1600 \text{ K} \)

\( T_{2} = 527\ ^\circ \text{C} = 527 + 273 = 800 \text{ K} \)

\( \dfrac{R_{1}}{R_{2}} = \left( \dfrac{T_{1}}{T_{2}} \right)^{4} = \left( \dfrac{1600}{800} \right)^{4} = 2^{4} = 16 \)

Discrimination — each option fixes a required temperature ratio \( \left( R_{1}/R_{2} \right)^{1/4} \): (A) needs \( 1.414 \), (C) needs \( 1.189 \), (D) needs \( 1.682 \), while the actual ratio is exactly \( 2 \). Only (B) matches. Option (C), \( 2 : 1 \), is the answer obtained by forgetting the fourth power, and using the Celsius values directly would give \( (1327/527)^{4} \approx 40 \), which matches no option at all.

Hence the ratio is \( 16 : 1 \) — option (B).
